summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on recurring schema assertion failures when using function-calling and structured output, plus observed latency variance tied to prefix KV cache settings. Redwood recommended a conservative kv ttl and prefix caching for common prompts, plus a structured fallback that routes to a quantized model when token latencies exceed thresholds. Action items assigned for config handoff, benchmark run, and a deeper technical follow-up next week.
transcript:
[15:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda, schema assertions, kv cache tweaks, and fallbacks. is that right rachel?
[15:06] Rachel Patel: yeah that works, thanks. Omar you had some failing examples from the last run?
[15:12] Omar Khan: yeah so, the main issue is when we call the invo-ke tool, function-calling, sometimes the model emits an array instead of the object, so our parser throws. it looks like about 3-4% of calls. we saw it both in staging and in the sandbox.
[15:30] Lucas Rivera: hm okay, are these mostly long context prompts or short? any pattern on token count?
[15:36] Omar Khan: mostly long — like 800 to 1k tokens. there's also some prefix repetition, like the system prompt repeats a nested list, and we suspect the KV cache maybe returning mismatched state.
[15:50] Maya Chen: right, we noticed KV cache TTL default was aggressive on your tenant, and with the continuous batching it can sometimes reuse partial KV entries. we call that K V cash in some logs, lol, the transcription spelled it weirdly before.
[16:00] Priya Desai: sorry quick question — when you say fallback to quantized model, does that change output quality? we need to make sure product isn't regressing.
[16:10] Lucas Rivera: good question. the fallback plan is tiered: first try prefix TTL increase and stricter assertion checks, if you hit an SLO threshold (p95 latency > 450ms or error rate spike) we route to a quantized variant that's functionally equivalent but lower cost and slightly higher variance in rare edge-cases. quality mostly intact for your templates, but we should validate on your golden prompts.
[16:26] Omar Khan: can you remind us where that routing policy lives? is it in the console or in a config file?
[16:30] Maya Chen: it's a routing policy in the pilot config — we send you the 'fallback-routes.yaml'. it's implemented in the control plane; for Dedicated pilot tenants we also install a local override in the runtime.
[16:42] Rachel Patel: okay, and about the schema assertion failures, is this something Redwood can auto-correct or do we need to change our parser to be tolerant?
[16:52] Lucas Rivera: there are a few approaches. one is to strengthen the model-side schema enforcement using the structured output 'assert' mode — we can have the model reformat on mismatch automatically and return a 2nd attempt. the other is to add a lightweight sanitizer in your SDK that runs an XSD-like check and attempts a small repair.
[17:08] Priya Desai: hmmm, the sanitizer sounds safer for us, but it adds latency. what's the tradeoff?
[17:14] Lucas Rivera: repair in SDK usually adds ~30-80ms depending on payload size. model-side reformat adds 150-300ms because it's a roundtrip. though model reformat keeps core logic centralized, fewer ad-hoc fixes.
[17:28] Omar Khan: for our throughput we care about p95 and cost. if we add SDK repair it'll be fine for correctness but increases compute on our side. can Redwood provide an example sanitizer?
[17:36] Maya Chen: yes, Lucas will provide a checklist and a small JS/Python sanitizer snippet. we'll include tests.
[17:42] Rachel Patel: another datapoint — during that 3% failure window we saw token spikes and the console shows repeated cache misses — could be misaligned KV keys.
[17:52] Lucas Rivera: that's consistent with our hypothesis. we can add a 'prefix normalization' step to your KV keys in the runtime or SDK. it normalizes whitespace and small punctuation differences in the prefix so cache hits improve.
[18:06] Priya Desai: do we risk over-normalizing and returning a wrong cached reply?
[18:10] Lucas Rivera: risk is low if we scope normalization to non-critical system prefixes; we can show you examples. safety first.
[18:18] Omar Khan: on benchmarking — we want to run a targeted 1k request test that exercises function-calling, structured output and a heavy prefix repetition case. we'll attach sample payloads.
[18:28] Maya Chen: perfect. we'll send the tuned KV and batching config. note: increase KV TTL from 45s to 180s for your pilot, enable prefix caching for top-3 templates, and set continuous batching max size to 16 for this workload.
[18:44] Rachel Patel: sounds good. is there any impact to costs if TTL is longer?
[18:50] Maya Chen: small increase in token cost for cache population but net decrease in model invocations for repeated prefixes, so overall cost usually drops. Lucas can model the economics for your traffic shape.
[18:58] Lucas Rivera: i'll run a quick cost/latency sim and attach a spreadsheet. also, send example traces — token-level traces help us see where KV lookup diverges.
[19:08] Priya Desai: ok next steps then?
[19:12] Maya Chen: recap — Maya sends config + docs, Lucas sends sanitizer checklist + cost sim, Omar runs 1k bench and shares traces, and we meet next week for the deep-dive. any other blockers?
[19:24] Omar Khan: just one: are there any known issues with SAML SSO for our users when we flip routing?
[19:30] Maya Chen: no, routing changes are at inference layer only, auth handshake is unchanged. we do a rollout in the control plane and keep user sessions intact.
[19:36] Rachel Patel: perfect. thanks everyone.
[19:40] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in the email thread with attachments.
[19:44] [Meeting ends]
